lessons.title: lunedì to venerdì — the planet-week, Italian-style
lessons.gloss: the weekdays (Monday–Friday) — the planets, with the day-word at the end

segments.text: Italy sat at the centre of the Roman world, so its weekday names are the planet-week almost undisturbed — the same map of the sky French uses. The tell is the little accented -dì at the end of each.
final-stress-i — the -dì carries a written accent and the stress: lu-ne-DÌ, mar-te-DÌ. That accent marks "day" (diēs) and where your voice lands.
c-before-i — mercoledì = mer-co-le-DÌ (hard c here, before o).
dì is Latin diēs, "day" — the same -di you'd hear in French lundi. Before it sits a planet-god:

utterances: Italian from Latin: lunedì from lūnae diēs. planet: Moon. Spanish / French twins: lunes / lundi.
Italian from Latin: martedì from Martis diēs. planet: Mars. Spanish / French twins: martes / mardi.
Italian from Latin: mercoledì from Mercuriī diēs. planet: Mercury. Spanish / French twins: miércoles / mercredi.
Italian from Latin: giovedì from Jovis diēs. planet: Jupiter (Giove). Spanish / French twins: jueves / jeudi.
Italian from Latin: venerdì from Veneris diēs. planet: Venus (Venere). Spanish / French twins: viernes / vendredi.

segments.text: Line up the three sisters — lunedì / lunes / lundi — and you have one Roman word, lūnae diēs, worn three ways. Italian and French keep the day-word at the end (lune-dì, lun-di); Spanish clipped it off entirely (lunes). And giovedì wears Giove, the Italian name of Jupiter — the same king-god English honours as Thor in Thursday.

[YOU SAY: "-dì = diēs = day" — the accented tail]

segments.text: What is the accented -dì, and from what Latin word? ("Day," from diēs.) Which planet is giovedì? (Jupiter — Giove.) How do Italian/French treat the day-word versus Spanish? (IT/FR keep it at the end, -dì/-di; Spanish dropped it, lunes.) Next: the weekend — Saturday and Sunday.

lessons.title: sabato and domenica — the religious weekend
lessons.gloss: the weekend (Saturday, Sunday) — Sabbath and the Lord's day

segments.text: The five weekdays were planets; the two weekend days are faith. Here the accented -dì disappears, because these names never came from diēs + a god — they came from the Sabbath and the Lord.

utterances: Italian from Latin: sabato from Sabbatum from Hebrew shabbāt. meaning: the "Sabbath," the day of rest. Spanish twin: sábado.
Italian from Latin: domenica from (diēs) Dominica from Dominus. meaning: "the Lord's day". Spanish twin: domingo.

segments.text: sabato is the Sabbath — Latin Sabbatum straight from Hebrew shabbāt, "to cease, to rest." Where English kept the planet (Saturday = Saturn), Italian, Spanish, and French all took the Jewish rest-day instead (sabato / sábado / samedi).

domenica is "the Lord's day," diēs Dominica, from Dominus "lord, master" ( becomes English dominion, dominate, dame, don). Christianity renamed the old "Sun's day": English still says Sunday, but Italian and Spanish point to the Lord (domenica / domingo). Note domenica is feminine (la domenica) — diēs went feminine here.

segments.text: Give all seven Italian days. (Lunedì … domenica.) Where does sabato come from? (The Sabbath, Sabbatum from Hebrew shabbāt.) What does domenica mean, and its Spanish twin? ("The Lord's day"; domingo.) Next chapter builds on this toward telling the time.
